lectures.title: What Jobs are and how to start your First Background Job (using `&`)

cues.en: In this lecture.
We want to have a look at background jobs in Bash.
But before we can look at background jobs, we should first clarify what exactly is a job in simple
terms.
A job is a command that is being executed.
Why do we have this distinction between a job and a process?
Well, the reason behind that one is that a job can consist of multiple programs.
So, for example, here we can see that two programs are connected to each other.
They are both running at the same time because they are connected to a pipe.
So that means both programs are running.
It's just that the output of this process here is connected to the input of this process here, and
this will then yield the result that we will see in our terminal.
But those are two processes.
But they are just one job in our bash terms because it's just one command that is being executed.
So in this case, we have two programs here, but only one job.
So, so far we have looked mostly at the so called foreground jobs.
Those pretty much occupy our shell in a sense that Bash will wait for their completion before accepting
a new command.
So in our shell, we can only have one foreground job at the same time.
But there's also a different kind of job, the so-called background jobs and those.
We will have a look at those here in this lecture.
So just to show you again, if I would start a program here, for example, the program ping to ping
a remote server, I could say ping, Google.com to send packages to Google and see how long it takes
to receive them back.
And then we can see here, this is now occupying my terminal.
We can see this because if I would now start typing here, for example, Ping, we can see this is not
really appearing in our shell.
I could now hit enter.
It's not going to get executed because this program ping is running here in our shell.
Or more appropriately to say this is a foreground job that's occupying our terminal and the bash will
wait for its completion.
This specific program here with those parameters will never complete.
But I could just hit control C to quit that job to send the corresponding signal here.
And now we can see here this job is now finished.
And now I am able to use my program or my my shell again.
I now just enter clear to clear my screen.
And this one here, for example, would now be this the first process and this would be the second process
that will be started.
They will just be linked, but still they will occupy my terminal, not because they generate output,

So this will run until I hit control C to send those signals to tell the to ask the process, hey,
please quit.

again.

Those are really great.
